title: The Truth About Dating Someone You're Not Meant to Marry
paragraphs:
The Truth About Dating Someone You're Not Meant to Marry
The relationship felt right. The feelings felt real. The chemistry felt undeniable. But what if the person you're holding onto is actually standing between you and God's best?
There is a kind of heartbreak that feels different from all the others.
Not because someone cheated.
Not because someone lied.
Not because the relationship was toxic.

But because deep down, beneath the laughter, the memories, the late-night conversations, the dreams, the plans, the promises, and the emotional attachment, there was a quiet voice you kept trying to silence.
A voice that kept whispering:
"This isn't the one."
And yet you stayed.
Maybe because leaving would hurt.
Maybe because being alone felt scarier.
Maybe because you invested too much already.
Maybe because you convinced yourself that if your feelings were strong enough, your future would somehow work itself out.
Many people are dating someone they were never meant to marry.
Not because God is cruel.
Not because they are bad people.
But because emotions can be loud while wisdom speaks softly.
And one of the hardest truths in life is that not every relationship is a divine appointment.
Some relationships are lessons.
Some relationships are mirrors.
Some relationships expose wounds that need healing.
Some relationships reveal idols hiding in the heart.
And some relationships exist only long enough for God to show you what cannot accompany you into your future.
That truth is uncomfortable.
Because we live in a culture that teaches us to follow our hearts.
Yet Scripture repeatedly warns us about the danger of allowing feelings to become our compass.
Jeremiah 17:9 says:
"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?"
The Hebrew word used for "deceitful" is עָקֹב (ʿaqob), carrying the idea of something crooked, elusive, or unreliable.
God is not saying emotions are evil.
He is saying emotions make terrible gods.
Because feelings can convince you that disobedience is love.
Feelings can convince you that compromise is wisdom.
Feelings can convince you to hold onto something God is asking you to release.
The most dangerous relationships are often not the obviously sinful ones.
They are the almost-right ones.
The ones where there is enough compatibility to keep you hopeful but enough spiritual conflict to keep you confused.
The ones where you constantly have to explain away warning signs.
The ones where your prayer life becomes weaker instead of stronger.
The ones where conviction becomes uncomfortable because it threatens what you want.
The ones where you slowly start negotiating with God.
One more month.
One more chance.
One more conversation.
One more sign.
One more reason to stay.
Yet every delay costs something.
Because every season spent holding onto the wrong person is a season unavailable for what God may be preparing next.
This does not mean every difficult relationship is wrong.
Marriage itself requires sacrifice, forgiveness, patience, and growth.
But there is a difference between working through challenges with someone moving toward Christ and constantly carrying a relationship that continually pulls you away from Him.
Amos 3:3 asks:
"Can two walk together, unless they are agreed?"
The Hebrew word behind "agreed" implies meeting by appointment, walking with shared direction and purpose.
The question is not merely whether two people love each other.
The question is whether they are walking toward the same King.
Because attraction cannot sustain what alignment was meant to carry.
Beauty fades.
Excitement fluctuates.
Chemistry rises and falls.
Life becomes difficult.
Children arrive.
Bills accumulate.
Health changes.
Trials emerge.
And when all the temporary things are stripped away, what remains is the foundation.
Jesus addressed foundations in Matthew 7:24-27.
The wise builder anchored everything on the rock.
The foolish builder built on sand.
Both houses looked fine for a season.
The storm revealed the difference.
Many relationships survive sunshine.
Few survive storms without Christ at the center.
And that is why some of the most painful breakups are actually acts of divine mercy.
Not punishment.
Mercy.
Because God sees the future you cannot see.
Isaiah 55:8-9 reminds us:
"For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD."
The Hebrew word for thoughts is מַחֲשָׁבוֹת (machashavot), referring to plans, intentions, purposes.
God is not merely thinking differently.
He is planning differently.
He knows what that relationship would eventually become.
He knows the compromises ahead.
He knows the spiritual battles ahead.
He knows the hidden pain ahead.
He knows what your future children may experience.
He knows what your calling requires.
And because He loves you, sometimes He closes doors you desperately wanted opened.
Not every closed door is rejection.
Sometimes it is rescue.
That is why so many believers eventually look back and thank God for relationships they once begged Him to save.
At the time it felt like devastation.
Years later it feels like protection.
Because hindsight often reveals what heartbreak concealed.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
Maybe you're still grieving someone.
Maybe you still replay conversations.
Maybe you still wonder what could have been.
Maybe part of you secretly hopes they come back.
But what if the greatest miracle is not reconciliation?
What if the greatest miracle is release?
What if God is not trying to restore the relationship?
What if He is trying to restore you?
Because before God gives you someone to walk beside, He often teaches you how to walk with Him.
The Greek word Jesus uses in Matthew 16:24 when He says, "Follow me," is ἀκολουθέω (akoloutheō).
It means to accompany, to walk the same road, to become a disciple.
Christianity has never been primarily about finding the right person.
It has always been about following the right Savior.
When Jesus becomes enough, everything changes.
You stop treating relationships like salvation.
You stop demanding from people what only God can provide.
You stop chasing validation.
You stop fearing loneliness.
You stop confusing attention with love.
You stop mistaking chemistry for covenant.
And suddenly your standards are no longer rooted in personal preference.
They are rooted in God's glory.
The truth is that the person you're not meant to marry can still teach you something valuable.
They can reveal your weaknesses.
They can expose your idols.
They can uncover areas needing healing.
They can show you how deeply you need Jesus.
Nothing is wasted in the hands of God.
Romans 8:28 remains true even in broken relationships.
Even in regret.
Even in disappointment.
Even in tears.
Even in endings.
God specializes in redemption.
The Gospel itself is proof.
Humanity rejected its Creator.
Sin fractured everything.
Shame entered the story.
The scandal of our rebellion should have been the end.
Instead, Jesus entered the story.
The cross became the place where justice and mercy embraced.
The empty tomb became the declaration that failure never gets the final word.
That is why our theme remains so powerful:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites broken stories.
He rewrites wasted years.
He rewrites wrong turns.
He rewrites heartbreak.
He rewrites regrets.
He rewrites shattered dreams.
He rewrites the chapters you wish never happened.
The enemy wants you trapped in what was.
Jesus calls you into what can be.
If this message stirred something deep within you, do not rush past it.
Sit with it.
Pray over it.
Ask God the difficult questions.
Ask Him whether you're holding onto something He is asking you to release.
Ask Him whether your relationship is moving you closer to Christ or farther from Him.
Ask Him to give you courage to obey even when obedience hurts.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Not because we are building a brand.
Because we are building disciples.
One day you may thank God for the relationship He removed more than the one you begged Him to keep.
